doc.title: Aebersold Jamey — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Isolation from Louisville, school band, and awareness of segregation
summary: Kimery asks about being isolated near Louisville; Aebersold describes bored sixth-grade band, Woolworth's lunches, and only a slight awareness of segregation.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Let’s talk about the community here, which is an interesting one, because you’re close to Louisville, but you’re definitely a distance away, so it’s not as easily accessible unless you have a driver’s license...
I’m not sure what public transportation was like at that time. But being a bigger city... You’re really, to some degree, a little bit isolated here.
So you’ve got to work twice as hard to be able to find those moments to develop your craft, or at least to find friends that had the same mind-frame.
Was there a group of kids that you ended up running with that were also musically inclined?

Yes. Band gave me that opportunity to meet other people. I tried to get the band director...Actually, let me back up. In the sixth grade, when I started... I went to Silver Street School up here, and kind of joined the band. I think we met once a week. I thought it was really boring. I’d already played piano, so I could read, and I had played some banjo, and it just seemed like the stuff we were doing was very simple, because I’m sure there were a lot of beginners there. So the band director was spending part of his time on just getting the kids to finger and blow the right note. And I’d already started listening to jazz. I remember that. So I said, “Well, it must be next year when I’m a seventh-grader,” down at the junior high school downtown, where you can ride your bike to school on a nice day, or ride the bus, and at lunchtime you can actually leave the building and go get a haircut if you want to, or go down to Woolworth’s and eat lunch... As a matter of fact, the Woolworth’s cafeteria in New Albany where I ate as a youngster was the first Woolworth cafeteria in America. I remember, for $1.05, I could get fried chicken,
green beans, mashed potatoes, rolls and a Coke. That was a big deal.
Can I ask you this. We’re talking about American history. This is still part of the segregated United States.
Was that something that you were aware of at that time?
